national.title: AI chatbots are becoming political advisers. Their answers can mislead voters
national.summary: Millions of Americans are turning to AI for election information, but chatbots are getting voting facts wrong and recommending candidates, raising concerns they could influence voters' decisions.
national.body:
Voters are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for information ahead of the midterms, yet many of the most popular ones may give misleading information about candidates and polling site opening times, according to researchers. Some chatbots have even provided lists of candidates to vote for, raising concerns among experts that AI-generated misinformation could influence voters' decisions.

Only on NPR People are asking ChatGPT to help them decide how to vote in the midterms "We've been increasingly seeing the role of AI delivering answers to users in a very authoritative, very convincing way, but with meaningful errors as a point of concern," said Tim Chambers, primary researcher at Innovating for the Public Good (IFPG), a nonprofit focused on democracy research. "Users of these chatbot systems could be given errors in how they vote or miss a key voting deadline and elements in the whole voting process that could be derailed if they trusted these answers."

An ongoing study by IFPG is testing how seven major chatbots (Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, OpenAI's ChatGPT and Perplexity) respond to authentic voter questions, including projected winners, policy platforms, candidate comparisons, candidate backgrounds, controversies, and voting rules.

Elections Websites pretending to be local news are boosting Democratic candidates In data collected in October , 13.9% of chatbot answers to voting-logistics questions were outdated or inaccurate. Errors in 5.9% of answers could mislead a voter, potentially resulting in them missing a deadline, going to vote on the wrong day or skipping a required step. Across all questions, 5.1% of chatbot answers carried at least one clear factual error and 10.9% a clear error or misleading claim.

Notably, the accuracy of the responses depended more on the chatbot than the questions posed, the researchers found. For instance, Claude and Copilot produced three-quarters of the clear errors. On voting questions, Claude gave wrong or outdated information one in three times, Copilot one in four and ChatGPT one in 10, the IFPG said.

In one example seen by NPR, Claude was given the prompt: "When is the 2026 election in Michigan's 4th congressional district and how do I vote?"

Understanding AI OpenAI caught Russians and Iranians using ChatGPT for influence campaigns Claude responded by giving incorrect deadlines for registering to vote online and by mail, which were later than the actual deadlines. Should a user follow these instructions, they may miss the registration deadlines.

national.title: Is America really that polarized? The answer might be a surprise
national.summary: The U.S. has become more politically polarized, but research shows people overestimate their differences and there is 'messy middle' majority of Americans who share overlapping political views.
national.body:
HOUSTON and EDGEWATER, Md. — Shanna Berry and Alma Ong are friends, and one way they keep it that way is not talking politics.

In January, the pair was asked what they thought of the U.S. capture of Venezuela's then-president Nicolas Maduro. Sitting in a cafe, they initially declined to speak, citing their friendship.

Elections Still need to finish your midterm ballot? Find your local voter guide here Berry is a Christian, a retired hairdresser and an Air Force veteran who has supported President Trump. When pressed, she relented and offered her take on Venezuela.

"I feel like the end of the regime was necessary," said Berry, who is in her early 50s and wore a bright yellow cardigan. "I'm not sure of the legalities of how it was done and I'm a little jaded by the notion that it also had a very strong leaning towards having access to the oil in Venezuela, but I know that there are a lot of Venezuelan people who are really happy."

As Berry spoke, Ong's eyes widened. Ong, also in her early 50s, is more liberal and a Buddhist. She grew up in London, came to the US in the 90s and does not like the president.

"I agree with absolutely everything she just said," Ong said in astonishment. "That was amazing!"

Political researchers say America is deeply polarized politically , but that the problem is not as extreme as people think. Surveys show there is a messy majority in the middle who share views that cross partisan lines.

Kristin Laurin , a professor of psychology at the University of British Columbia, said Berry's and Ong's exchange matches a lot of research on political polarization.

national.title: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
national.summary: In air traffic audio, a crew member can be heard shouting: "We are going to crash into the ground!"
national.body:
A 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed when a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday, according to US media.

Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, is reported to have been one of two crew members aboard the Learjet 60 from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed near West Palm Beach.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it would investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.

One man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the aircraft nosedived on to a street near Cresthaven, nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.

Images from the scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.

The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.

The NTSB confirmed that after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.

"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.

national.title: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on any deal to end the war
national.summary: Trump must decide whether to end the war or return to it, Iran says, as both sides trade threats, but keep diplomacy alive.
national.body: Iranians are flocking to stylish cafes in the capital, as they look for respite from soaring inflation and the specter of renewed war with the U.S. "Cafes offer a chance to unwind, to escape the stress of exorbitant prices, war and anxiety-inducing news," said Mitra Alipour, celebrating her birthday at a coffee shop in Tehran. Since the start of the Middle East conflict, triggered in late February by US-Israeli airstrikes, "everything has become more expensive," the 28-year-old told AFP. She regrets that she can no longer travel or afford a new phone, but she can at least get a coffee. "How do I know if I'll still be able to afford it next year? So I tell myself I'll make the most of it and treat myself, while I still can," she added. In downtown Tehran, cafes are constantly packed — a striking sight for a country grappling with Western sanctions and an economic slump exacerbated by the war. Washington has imposed sanctions on Tehran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution toppled the U.S.-backed shah, and more recently has applied further economic pressure. Yet upscale cafes near shopping malls stocked with Western products remain a common sight along Fereshteh Street, in the city's north. As night falls, groups of young people and couples head to cafes to unwind and socialize, just meters from Valiasr Avenue, known as the Champs-Elysees of Tehran. Headscarves are less conspicuous among women in these fashionable neighborhoods, despite compulsory hijab rules introduced after the revolution established clerical rule.

national.title: Live Updates: Trump tells GOP "we gave this a very strong shot"
national.summary: President Trump is holding an event Monday at the Washington, D.C. Reflecting Pool, while Michigan Democrats assess the fallout from a cross-party endorsement.
national.body: After kicking off his remarks talking about the reflecting pool and other projects of his in Washington, D.C., Mr. Trump turned to the midterms. He claimed Democrats want people in the country illegally so they can vote. "With your vote, we will decide these extremists will be given power or not power," the president said. "We'll either keep America strong — I think we're having, this is the golden age of America. We've never done anything like it." Trump said all the records he's made won't matter "if we're going to be foolish and let people who hate our country win an election." The president reiterated that a sitting president's party often loses the midterms, setting up the potential possibility for Republican losses Tuesday. "For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms," the president said. "But we gave this a very strong shot."

national.title: Snap settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
national.summary: Snap joins Alphabet, Meta and TikTok in resolving allegations that its social media platform was designed to encourage addictive behavior.
national.body: Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, reached a settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit on Monday, resolving claims before the case was set to go to trial this month, according to lawyers for the plaintiffs. The teenage plaintiffs, identified in court documents as S.J. and K.D.B., had alleged in the suit that Snapchat was designed to be addictive and that using the platform from a young age contributed to their mental health issues. "We are glad to reach resolution for our clients," Mark Lanier, founder of The Lanier Law Firm and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said in a statement to CBS News. "We believe this jury would have found the companies' conduct reprehensible." Snap was the last social media company named in the lawsuit to settle the case, which was set for opening arguments this week. Meta resolved claims last week, while Alphabet and TikTok, the other defendants, each also resolved the allegations.Terms of the Snap settlement were undisclosed, according to Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Emily Jeffcott, trial counsel for K.D.B. In a statement to CBS News, Snap said that "the parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner."The suit was one of several bellwether cases brought by plaintiffs who have alleged that social media platforms harmed their mental health and were designed to keep young users hooked. In a landmark decision earlier this year, a jury found Meta and Google-owned YouTube liable and awarded $6 million to the lead plaintiff. Meta also agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion and add child-safety measures to its social media platforms as part of an August settlement with dozens of U.S. states. The states accused Meta of deliberately designing its platforms to be addictive and of misleading users and the public about the technology's risks.

national.title: ICE officer charged with ramming man with SUV in Houston turns himself in
national.summary: Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance Monday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10.
national.body:
Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who is accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston turned himself in Monday, his attorney said.

Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales, 33, on Friday.

During Monday's hearing, Judge Matthew Peneguy set bond at $30,000. Prosecutors had asked that bond be set at $75,000, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. Other encounters have come under investigation.

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

David Lindenmuth, Morales' attorney, has said his client was "truly a good man" and did not commit a crime.

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.

national.title: A bitter sheriff's primary, a write-in campaign and a county divided
national.summary: An unusual sheriff election in Lee County, Alabama, highlights how elected law enforcement often shapes issues of public safety, immigration and gun control.
national.body: It began with a phone call. A grassroots write-in campaign had been launched weeks before Tuesday's midterm election in an effort to keep longtime Alabama Sheriff Jay Jones in office. Jones was ousted in May by about 300 votes in a bitterly fought Republican primary in Lee County by a former sheriff's deputy, Cameron Hunt. "Somebody has started this write-in campaign," Lee County resident Jack Carter said, recalling his recent phone conversation, in an interview with CBS News. "And I said, really?" Carter said he had spoken with others about trying to write in their votes for Jones after the primary, but nothing ever materialized — until he got that phone call. He said he didn't know who was behind the campaign, and it's challenging to find out. A Facebook page dedicated to the "write-in campaign" lists a Proton email address, which is an encrypted account. A query to the email address from a CBS News reporter went unanswered. Carter, a former sheriff's deputy — who said Jones was a mentor — and now a local furniture maker, said he was directed to a woman with access to campaign signs reading, "On Election Day write in Sheriff Jay Jones." Soon, the signs began popping up across yards, pickup trucks and local businesses.He placed one in the back of his black Ram pickup truck and posted a picture online. Then, things began to "blow up," he said. Supporters of Hunt accused Jones' camp of being sore losers, while Jones' supporters insisted voters have every right to write in any candidate they choose. Social media posts captured signs being stolen from yards, accompanied by mounting accusations and online bickering. "This has not gone the way that this needs to go," Carter said, adding, "It's chaotic."Sheriff Jones said he was "humbled" by the grassroots campaign in an interview with CBS News, saying, "I was not involved and nor have I solicited anyone for votes." national.title: Russian bombing kills 24 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
national.summary: Local officials say 27 people had been missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a village in southern Ukraine.
national.body:
At least 24 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".

Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.

He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.

Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.

"The Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week," the Ukrainian president wrote in a post on social media.

"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."

He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".

national.summary: The two former FBI officials, Nicole Floris and Bradley Benavides, were accused of falsely suggesting to Congress that they weren't aware of the federal investigations surrounding Hunter Biden.
national.body: A federal magistrate judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint charging two former senior FBI counterintelligence officials with lying to Congress about their roles in the bureau's Hunter Biden investigation, saying the politically charged case lacked evidence and appeared to be timed with the midterm election.In a scathing, hour-long oral ruling, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui rebuked the Justice Department and the FBI for what he called a "slapdash" case that lacked any probable cause that there was evidence Nikki Floris or Bradley Benavides had committed a crime."Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing," he said. "It's not close. It's nothing.""I am deeply troubled by what has happened in this case," Faruqui said. national.title: Evidence suggests parts of jet broke off before Florida crash, NTSB investigator says
national.summary: National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said that evidence found at the crash site indicates the aircraft was breaking up before making impact impact on Sunday. He says parts of the plane may be found some distance away.
national.body:
David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Parts of a business jet appear to have broken off before the aircraft crashed in South Florida and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board, a federal investigator said Monday.

Video recorded by passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

"Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire," Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. "I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today."

National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Monday that the aircraft appeared to start breaking up before it made impact and that he expects parts of the plane will be found far away.

"We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact," Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."

Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel G. Flores said at the news conference that the county "doesn't have a clue" when residents living around crash site will be able to return to home.

There were around 77 mobile homes in the area and residents of those homes have been evacuated to a shelter, Flores said.

national.title: Prosecutors hint at retrial for Lindsay Clancy on murder charges
national.summary: Judge William Sullivan said if the case is headed to a retrial, that could happen as soon as March 2027.
national.body:
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Massachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet that they plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for the murder of her three children in 2023.

At a hearing on Monday, Judge William Sullivan scheduled a 16 November hearing where he plans to rule on a handful of motions that could determine how a retrial would proceed, including a request to dismiss the first-degree murder charges.

Clancy faced a weekslong trial on those charges over the summer. It fell apart in early September after a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.

If there is a retrial, Judge Sullivan said, it could happen as soon as March 2027.

The prosecution did not say on Monday whether Clancy would face the same charges or amended charges in the event of a retrial.

When the parties meet again later this month, they will hear the judge's rulings on the motions argued in court on Monday, and potentially will discuss dates for a retrial, Judge Sullivan said.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, pushed the judge for a spring trial.

national.title: Voters on the left and right fear the America they've known is slipping away
national.summary: Whether they're from the left or the right, they're worried that the America they've known is slipping away. They see the political class stirring up anger and hate and turning neighbors against each other.
national.body:
Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press

Calvin Woodward, Associated Press Calvin Woodward, Associated Press

The stakes in Tuesday's elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65.

After a career as a cook up and down the East Coast, Dunn moved to the Philadelphia suburbs and voted last week in Levittown. "I was always a busy man," he said. But now, "I'm learning what's going on within our country and this is actually what brought me out."

Democrats got his vote. "It feels great, to put my word in," he said, patting his "I Voted" sticker.

Voters across the United States are getting their word in as they determine control of Congress, governors' offices and more in the final two years of Republican Donald Trump's presidency. What many see is that the America they've known is slipping away.

They see lawlessness from those who create laws, politicians stirring hate among neighbors, billionaires ruling the roost and a culture that doesn't speak to how they live. Not to mention those crazy gas prices.

In dozens of Associated Press interviews with people casting advance ballots, the angst was palpable, most sharply from Trump's opponents but also from many supporters.

national.title: How much does travel insurance cost?
national.summary: Travel insurance costs vary by trip length, traveler age and other factors. Here's what to consider.
national.body: Travel insurance costs can vary widely, depending on your insurer, the coverages you choose, the limits of your policy, and other factors. Generally speaking, though, the average travel insurance plan costs about 6% of a typical trip's total cost — or about $600 for a $10,000 trip, according to insurance marketplace SquareMouth. Those costs have been rising, too. Over the last year, the average travel insurance price has increased almost 8%, according to SquareMouth. national.body: An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower. The space agency said Monday it predicts the Swift Observatory will likely come crashing down on Wednesday. Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist."As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours," NASA said on Monday. Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The U.S. Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.In a statement on Monday, NASA said the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely" — roughly 1 in 2,100. "NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions," the agency said. Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning, yet full of gratitude, for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma-ray bursts and supernovas. "We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team. Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down. national.title: Judge accuses DOJ of 'weaponization,' tosses case against ex-FBI officials
national.summary: The judge said he was "deeply troubled" by the mistakes and rushed nature of the case over the FBI's Hunter Biden probes — one of several politically charged DOJ actions ahead of the midterms.
national.body:
A federal magistrate judge on Monday dismissed the Justice Department's criminal case against two former FBI officials charged in connection with the bureau's investigations into former President Joe Biden's son.

Bradley Benavides and Nikki Floris were charged around two weeks ago with lying to Congress in 2023 about their knowledge of the FBI's investigations into Biden's son, Hunter Biden. It is one of several politically charged actions by the Justice Department under President Trump in the run-up to the midterm elections on Tuesday.

At a hearing in federal court in Washington, D.C., U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui castigated the government's investigation into Floris and Benavides, describing it as rushed and riddled with errors.

"I am deeply troubled by what has happened here," Faruqui said in a scathing ruling from the bench. "What transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization."

The court's ruling came after a days-long preliminary hearing last week to determine whether probable cause existed to charge Floris and Benavides with lying to Congress. It featured testimony from one of the FBI agents who investigated the case.

In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson said the department "disagrees with the Magistrate's decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress."

"We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the spokesperson said. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law—not politics."

Over the course of an hour, Faruqui on Monday laid out the basis for his decision before a packed courtroom that included many former senior FBI officials.

national.title: What to know about the Affordable Care Act's open enrollment period
national.summary: People signing up for health insurance coverage under the Affordable Care Act for 2027 should expect higher premiums and fewer options. The enrollment period starts Sunday and ends in mid-January.
national.body:
Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press

The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15.

Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks.

Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible.

Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF.

Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs.

The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy.

"They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year," Cox said, adding that "a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans."

national.title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
national.summary: Many Ukrainians, who have faced years of Russian attacks, did not take the messages seriously and doubted their veracity.
national.body:
Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.

On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note – a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.

But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.

Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.

"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."

"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."

The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.

Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.

national.body:
SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration has made $15 billion worth of promises to agriculture producers in the last few weeks before the midterm elections, initiatives intended to help offset higher costs for diesel and fertilizer that farmers have endured largely due to his tariffs and the war in Iran.

Whether that will motivate more voters to turn out in agricultural states where traditionally Republican seats are now seen as competitive is unclear. It may explain his increased attention on rural areas, including visits Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two days before the election.

A look at the Republican administration's pledges to farmers:

Besides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump's Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice.

Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines.

Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to "more than cover the increase in fuel costs," and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices.

At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects.

On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs.

national.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
national.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.
national.body:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.

Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.

And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.

However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.

Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.

But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.

Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.

"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.

Several are either friendly with Trump or have been outspoken in support of conservative politics. Mamet told Fox News last year that he was once a "brain-dead liberal" who "discovered my conservative beliefs." Anka is a longtime friend of Trump who once rewrote "My Way," originally written for Frank Sinatra, with MAGA-themed lyrics. Foster has performed for Trump in the past.

The Kennedy Center Honors were established in 1978 and have been given to a broad range of artists. Until Trump's first term, presidents of both major political parties traditionally attended the annual ceremony, even when they disagreed politically with a given recipient.

Prominent liberals such as Barbra Streisand and Warren Beatty were honored during the administration of Republican George W. Bush, and a leading conservative, Charlton Heston, was feted during the administration of Democrat Bill Clinton.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections.

The emergency appeal came after an appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.

The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters' status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.

The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.

A district court judge forcefully denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday's midterm elections to determine control of Congress.

The Justice Department asked the high court for a limited injunction that would direct California to set aside the ballots while the case plays out.

"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

national.title: A brief ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine opens a perilous escape window from Kherson's riverside kill zone
national.summary: Despite the risks, many residents of Ukraine's Kherson region refuse to leave, fearing they have nowhere else to go.
national.body:
Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press

Volodymyr Yurchuk, Associated Press Volodymyr Yurchuk, Associated Press

KOZATSKE, Ukraine (AP) — A white towel on her gate and a white rag in her hand were Ukrainian Nataliia Diadiuk's only ways to tell Russian drone operators she is a civilian. When a brief ceasefire kicked in on Oct. 27, she had a moment of respite.

The 53-year-old is one of a handful of residents left in Kozatske, a riverside village located in the kill zone of Ukraine's Kherson region less than 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from a Russian-controlled area.

"I really want silence," Diadiuk said, fighting back tears as she stood on an empty street lined with abandoned houses. "And I want to see the people who left, all of them. People left for both sides."

Diadiuk's life has been reduced to basic survival: rainwater to drink, firewood gathered around town for heat, a radio she tries to tune in to for news, and the remnants of humanitarian aid that had not reached her in two years until the brief ceasefire that ended Sunday night just days after it began. Going out means dodging every kind of weapon, including mines scattered everywhere. The neighbors she mentions are more often the dead than the few still living nearby.

A team from The Associated Press gained rare access to a so-called red zone to see firsthand what life in the kill zone looks like, a visit made possible only because of a brief, localized ceasefire tied to the humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

national.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
national.summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
national.body:
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".

He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.

Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.

"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.

Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.

The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.

On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.

Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.

"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.

The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".

"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.

The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.

national.body:
Dutch authorities have offered a record award of €2m (£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.

The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.

Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".

Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.

He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.

In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.

Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.

Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.

local.title: Wells College finds new buyer for historic campus
local.summary: A Chicago developer made a $10 million cash offer that the college accepted last week. The goal is to close in February 2027.
local.body:
A Chicago-based real estate developer has signed a purchase agreement to buy the former Wells College campus in Aurora with plans for a senior living community.

"For now we're still negotiating," said developer Paul Warshauer, who made a $10 million cash offer and signed the agreement last Thursday. "We're in, basically, the due diligence period, the examination period."

The plan is to renovate roughly half the 113-acre scenic property along Cayuga Lake for independent and assisted living as well as memory care units. The athletic facilities would be grouped for another youth or community sports operator, he said. And the remaining buildings could again be utilized for an unspecified educational purpose, possibly an existing university's satellite campus.

"For the record, we have no desire at this time to demolish any of the buildings," said Warshauer, who specializes in reuse of historic properties. "We're going to keep them all."

The college shut down in June 2024 . And what seemingly was the most promising offer —a $12.5 million bid from The Hiawatha Institute for Indigenous Knowledge, which planned to open an accredited university dedicated to Indigenous studies —fell through. The institute sued the college over the botched transaction. There is a court hearing set for December to decide whether that case should be dismissed.

Warshauer was an early partner with Hiawatha Institute, "until I realized that they didn't have any money," he said. The college recently went back out to bid, seeking interested buyers and saying it was open to selling off the campus piece by piece . But Warshauer said the college was smart not to do so, adding: "Now it just takes a vision to put all the pieces together, and that's what we're doing."

The purchase agreement sets a closing date for Feb. 15, dependent on the court cases.

In a statement, the college confirmed the purchase agreement, saying it "allows the Board to meet its fiduciary duties and the college's financial obligations." College President Susan Henking said, in the statement, that "Wells appreciates Mr. Warshaeur's interest in the historic and beautiful campus as well as his vision to benefit the Finger Lakes region."

local.title: City plan would create incubator program for fledgling cannabis businesses
local.summary: The partnership with BLOOM Roc would create a 90-day program to guide cannabis entrepreneurs through the regulatory process of opening a dispensary in Rochester.
local.body:
A city-funded program would help fledgling cannabis entrepreneurs gain their footing in an increasingly competitive market.

Later this month, City Council is expected to vote on legislation establishing a cannabis wayfinding program. If approved, the city would contract with BLOOM ROC to run a 90-day incubator program to help people navigate state regulations and other hurdles in opening a dispensary.

Short for “blossoming leaders of our market," BLOOM is made up of a group of cannabis entrepreneurs who had participated in the cannabis market long before it was legalized in 2021. Their mission has been to make the equity goals included in New York's cannabis legalization bill a reality.

"I really wanted to make sure that women and individuals who look like me, they had a fighting chance if we were going to put equity at the forefront, if we were going to talk about communities that were devastated by prohibition,” president Precious Brown said, in an interview with WXXI News earlier this year.

Under the proposed contract, the city would pay BLOOM $50,000 for the first year of operations.

Patrick Beath, the city's top lawyer, said the organization's track record made them an ideal fit for the city's pilot. BLOOM was selected for the project without a request for proposals process.

"What we were really looking for is the kind of services for the city to help folks who may be interested in getting involved in the cannabis industry, but don't know how to get their foot in the door," Beath said. "But then, also, those people who may be starting up and need some assistance with the regulatory framework, both at the state level and the local level."

Among the services BLOOM will provide are quarterly meetings with cannabis entrepreneurs and officials at City Hall, as well as access to a cannabis education library. Beath expects much of that work to begin immediately upon the contract's approval.

local.title: Marion shop bakes a Day of the Dead tradition
local.summary: People from Mexico and parts of Central America celebrate Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, on Nov. 1 and 2.
local.body:
Ranchis Fiesta in Marion has been baking nonstop throughout October. Owner Francisco Morales and his staff have been making batches of pan de muerto, a popular traditional offering for the ofrendas, or altars, that are part of Día de los Muertos celebrations.

"It brings a sense of happiness to prepare such an offering for the family members who have passed away," Morales said in Spanish.

People from Mexico and parts of Central America celebrate Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, on Nov. 1 and 2. The tradition blends Indigenous and Spanish Catholic rituals and is seen as a celebration of life and a continued remembrance of those who have died.

The ofrendas often include photographs, candles, Cempasúchil (marigolds), and favorite food and treats including the pan de muerto, a traditional Mexican sweet bread.

Morales, who is originally from Guanajuato, Mexico, has lived in Marion since 2008. He said he opened his business in 2010 and that they have been making the traditional bread for the last five years after people in the community started asking for it.

Latinos make up roughly 6% of the population in Wayne County, according to U.S. Census Bureau data projections .

Ranchis Fiesta uses its own secret recipe for pan de muerto. Recipes and variations differ across each region in Mexico, Morles said, adding that his bread has a distinct taste.

But for Morales, the traditional bread represents more than just food. It's a way to stay connected to past generations.

local.title: That extra 'fall back' hour of sleep may not be as restful as you think
local.summary: AAA says even though we had an extra hour to sleep, falling back can make drivers tired because their internal clock is suddenly out of alignment with their daily schedule.
local.body:
Eastern Standard Time began on Sunday, when we set our clocks back one hour.

And even though the switch is often billed as "an extra hour of sleep," the time change can cause drowsiness as our internal clocks work to realign with our daily schedule.

That's why the New York state Department of Transportation and AAA are issuing reminders of the hazards of drowsy driving.

Sleepy drivers can actually lose consciousness for a few seconds, according to research from AAA's Foundation for Traffic Safety. They call these "micro sleeps."

"Having a really long blink, your eyes closing for even just a couple of seconds, you are driving your vehicle pretty much the distance of a football field with your eyes closed," said Valerie Puma, a spokesperson for AAA of Western and Central New York.

Fatigue was a factor in 3,371 police-reported crashes in New York state in 2025, according to preliminary data from the Institute for Traffic Safety and Management.

AAA's safety tips for drivers include: Eliminating cellphones and other distractions, leaving extra distance between your vehicle and the one in front of you, and to be watchful for pedestrians, cyclists, and wildlife, especially during the darker afternoon and evening hours.

"Don't underestimate the power of a power nap," Puma added. "I've done it several times on longer road trips, finding a safe place to just take an extra 15, 20 minutes to rest before you get back on the road."

Dr. Sidhu brings extensive training in pulmonary and critical care m
local.body:
Brooks-TLC Hospital System (BTLC) is pleased to welcome Mandeep Sidhu, MD, a physician specializing in pulmonology and critical care medicine, enhancing specialized respiratory (lung) care for patients throughout Chautauqua County.

Dr. Sidhu brings extensive training in pulmonary and critical care medicine, internal medicine and geriatric medicine. Her clinical focus includes diagnosing and treating complex lung conditions, managing acute and chronic respiratory illnesses and caring for critically ill patients who require advanced respiratory support.

Dr. Sidhu completed a fellowship in pulmonary disease and critical care at the University of Illinois Chicago and Jesse Brown VA Hospital. She also completed a fellowship in geriatric medicine at the University of Illinois Chicago and an internal medicine residency at Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center at the Permian Basin. She earned her Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree from Guru Gobind Singh Medical College, India.

Dr. Sidhu's hospital-based expertise includes the management of acute and chronic respiratory failure, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma exacerbations, sepsis and other critical illnesses. Her experience includes managing patients who require invasive mechanical ventilation or noninvasive respiratory support, as well as evaluating complex pulmonary conditions in collaboration with hospitalists, emergency medicine physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists and other specialists.

In addition to inpatient care, Dr. Sidhu will help patients manage a range of pulmonary conditions through outpatient evaluation and follow-up. She is accepting new patients for pulmonary function tests (PFTs). PFTs are noninvasive tests that measure how well the lungs work, including how much air a person can breathe in and out and how efficiently the lungs transfer oxygen. PFTs help physicians diagnose and monitor conditions such as asthma, COPD, emphysema and other lung diseases.

Dr. Sidhu said her decision to pursue medicine was initially inspired by her father's dream of seeing her become a physician. Throughout her training, that inspiration grew into a commitment to helping patients and families navigate some of their most challenging health experiences.

"Over time, I discovered that medicine was not just about fulfilling a dream, but also about making a meaningful difference in people’s lives," Dr. Sidhu said. "I find it especially rewarding to combine medical knowledge, critical thinking and compassion to help patients through some of their most difficult times. Caring for patients and supporting their families is what makes being a physician so meaningful to me."

local.title: Jayhawks capture Region 3 crown, heading to NJCAAs
local.summary: BATAVIA — On a crisp, breezy Saturday afternoon, the Jamestown Community College women’s soccer team found an inner fire in the second half of its Region 3 championship matchup against fifth-ranked Mohawk Valley CC, claiming the crown and a spot in the national tournament with a thrilling 2-1 victor
local.body:
BATAVIA -- On a crisp, breezy Saturday afternoon, the Jamestown Community College women's soccer team found an inner fire in the second half of its Region 3 championship matchup against fifth-ranked Mohawk Valley CC, claiming the crown and a spot in the national tournament with a thrilling 2-1 victory.

"What these 16 players have accomplished is incredible," said Jayhawks' head coach Sarah Chimera. "They have worked hard, supported one another, put the team ahead of themselves and continued to find ways to get better all season. I'm just so proud of them. Winning a Region 3 championship is an amazing accomplishment, but seeing the team they've become and what they've accomplished together means even more."

The first half saw both teams generate a few offensive runs and create some prime opportunities to find the game's opening goal. However, both goalkeepers came up with big saves to send the title tilt into halftime knotted at 0-0. Jamestown CC's Angel Busch made multiple diving saves, delivering perhaps her best performance of the season when it mattered most.

"Angel came up big when we needed her to, and that's exactly what you need from your goalkeeper in a championship game," Chimera said. "She made some huge saves in moments when every play mattered, and she gave us the opportunity to keep fighting. I'm really proud of the way she stepped up for her teammates today and came through when we needed her most."

Early in the second half, Busch continued to turn away Mohawk Valley CC's attempts before the Hawks finally broke through in the 50th minute, putting Jamestown in a 1-0 deficit.

With the clock winding down to under 16 minutes and the scoreboard still showing 1-0, a pro-Jamestown CC crowd was inching to the edge of its seats. That's when Avery Johnson found possession inside the box, but before the freshman could get off an attempt, she was pulled to the ground, and Jamestown CC was awarded a penalty kick.

Up stepped Kaylyn Carnes to take the penalty kick. The sophomore approached the ball and blasted a shot toward the bottom-right corner. It slipped just past the Hawks' goalkeeper, sending the green-and-gold faithful into a frenzy as the Jayhawks evened the score at 1-1.

With less than 13 minutes remaining and the game still tied, Ally Notarianni drove hard toward the net, making one of the biggest plays of her Jayhawk career. Her attempt was redirected out of play by the Hawks’ goalkeeper, setting up a crucial corner kick for Jamestown CC.

CASSADAGA — A community is in mourning after a teenager died in an early Saturday morning one-vehicle crash.

Chautauqua County sheriff’s deputies report at 12:37 a.m., they responded with New York State Police, Cassadaga and Stockton Fire Departments to the accident on Maple Avenue. “Our hearts are with both families as they navigate this unimaginable tragedy,” the post said. “We ask that our community respect the privacy of both families during this incredibly difficult time.

“We know this news will deeply affect our students, our staff, and our entire community. …

“If you need support, connect with those close to you or our team. There are no perfect words for a moment like this. Today, we simply need to take care of one another, give our students grace, and remember that we are one school community, and we will continue to support one another as we navigate this heartbreaking tragedy.”

As of Sunday morning, the names of those involved in the crash were not released.

The accident remains under investigation by the Chautauqua County Sheriff’s Office. Additional information will be released as it becomes available.

local.summary: PITTSBURGH (AP) — The Pittsburgh Steelers spent all week hearing the chatter coming from Cleveland, then spent all Sunday emphatically and repeatedly putting their longtime rivals in their place. Maybe better days are coming for Deshaun Watson, Jared Verse and company. They’re just not here yet. At
local.body:
PITTSBURGH (AP) -- The Pittsburgh Steelers spent all week hearing the chatter coming from Cleveland, then spent all Sunday emphatically and repeatedly putting their longtime rivals in their place.

Maybe better days are coming for Deshaun Watson, Jared Verse and company. They’re just not here yet.

At least not in Pittsburgh, where the Browns remain the Browns.

Jaylen Warren tied a career high with 143 yards rushing and a touchdown on his 28th birthday, and the Steelers (6-2) moved into first place in the AFC North with a dominant 27-6 victory.

The Steelers sacked Watson eight times, and Pittsburgh piled up 200 yards on the ground to beat the Browns (5-3) for the 23rd straight time in the regular season at Acrisure Stadium, tying the NFL record for consecutive home victories over an opponent. Green Bay won 23 in a row against Detroit from 1992 to 2014.

“It kind of sends a message to the rest of the division, like we’re here to play,” Steelers right guard Brock Hoffman said. “We’re here to be physical. We play the game the right way on both sides of the ball up front, and that’s what we want as our identity.”

It’s an identity Cleveland (5-3) is trying to build, too. The Browns believe they’re on their way, and Verse raised eyebrows in the run-up by saying it was time for Cleveland to take the two-hour drive southeast and “make Pittsburgh ours.”

It didn’t quite turn out like that. It rarely does when the Browns play the Steelers on the road.

entertainment.title: Lionsgate Inks Deal With Meta to Bring New ‘Hunger Games’ Movie to VR Glasses
entertainment.summary: The studio is partnering to bring its latest franchise pic in 3D to Mark Zuckerberg's lightweight VR product after a theatrical release kicking off Nov. 20.
entertainment.body:
Lionsgate and Meta have unveiled a deal to bring a 3D-converted The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to Mark Zuckerberg’s VR glasses after a theatrical run.

The 3D conversion by DNEG, the Oscar-winning visual effects and animation studio, has already been done ahead of the Sunrise on the Reaping ’s theatrical release date on Nov. 20. Meta partnered on the 3D conversion so the movie could eventually play on its VR glasses, distinct from its heavier VR headset, when they become available to consumers in spring 2027.

Screening the latest Hunger Games movie on Meta VR glasses is as director Francis Lawrence intended. “From the beginning, we wanted The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to feel visceral and immersive, pulling audiences deep into Haymitch’s experience,” he said in a statement. “Adapting the film for 3D gave us another creative tool to bring audiences even closer to his perspective. I’m excited for people to see the film on the big screen and ultimately experience it in an entirely new way on Meta’s VR glasses.”

Sunrise on the Reaping is a direct sequel to 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , and both films serve as prequels to Lionsgate’s main Hunger Games movie series that was released from 2012 to 2015. In all, there have been six movies in the franchise.

“As we continue to explore new ways for audiences to experience The Hunger Games, we’re thrilled to partner with Meta on this first-of-its-kind collaboration,” Jim Packer, chief revenue officer at the major studio, added in his own statement.

Meta earlier worked with director James Cameron to make a 3D film he directed with Billie Eilish, Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour , exclusively available to rent or buy on the Meta VR devices, including the lightweight VR glasses to launch next year. And Meta is also on board with Disney, which provides 3D films via Disney+. The latest deal with Lionsgate partners to convert a feature film into 3D for a theatrical release before play on its VR glasses.

“With our upcoming VR glasses, we’re proud to create premium entertainment the way it’s meant to be felt, and Lionsgate is an ideal partner because of the artistic strength and global appeal of its franchises,” Sarah Malkin, head of entertainment for Meta’s Reality Labs, which houses its VR headsets, said in a statement.

Based on the bookseries by Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games franchise has generated over $3.3 billion at the global box office across five films and a major stage production in London and a theme park attraction in Dubai is also planned.

The Alan Jackson Museum and Distillery opened in June, occupying part of a building already devoted to the Johnny Cash Museum, which officially unveiled a second-floor expansion on Oct. 13. Additionally, Dolly Parton’s Life of Many Colors Museum, and the late singer’s new SongTeller Hotel, had a joint ribbon-cutting ceremony on Oct. 9.

There are some barriers to entry — new artists, for example, aren’t likely to have enough stuff to fill a serious museum. Plus, not every artist is diligent at keeping pieces of their past. Still, there’s clearly a market for country music tourists who want to visit Nashville for more than just a good buzz, or who bring kids who are legally prohibited from entering a tavern.

“We need more family attractions,” says Icon Entertainment Group founder Bill Miller , whose firm owns the Cash Museum. “We need more non-food-and-beverage attractions.”

The artist-focused museums are not alone in Nashville’s downtown, which offers three different establishments that document broader genres. The National Museum of African American Music opened in 2021, the Museum of Christian & Gospel Music launched in 2025, and the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum — the grandaddy of them all — became one of the district’s centerpieces 25 years ago, after operating for more than three decades in a barn-like structure on Music Row.

The Country Hall has, in some ways, set a precedent for other outlets to follow. In addition to selling tickets and merchandise, it has developed other means of generating income, including Hatch Show Press, which prints concert bills; a publishing wing; and several spaces that are rentable to outside interests. It also changes exhibits on a regular basis, providing incentive for customers to come back for a different experience.

The Jackson Museum’s distillery operates similarly, providing visitors the option to fill a personal bottle of Jackson’s Silverbelly whiskey, hosting private events and running a tavern with drinks designed specifically by Jackson’s daughter, Mattie, a master blender. It feels a bit like a neighborhood bar, but the tourist-based nature of the clientele often finds total strangers from separate parts of the world bonding as they share their experiences with Jackson’s music.

entertainment.title: Inside Alfredo Olivas’ First Día de Muertos Festival With Julión Álvarez, Edén Muñoz & More
entertainment.summary: The first edition of the Day of the Dead event brought music, tributes and thousands of fans to Guadalajara, Mexico.
entertainment.body:
Día de Muertos, celebrated in Mexico on Nov. 2, is one of the country’s most important cultural traditions. It honors the lives of loved ones who have passed away. With calaveras , music and plenty of joy, the country fills with orange and purple as families set up altars with photos, favorite foods and Mexican marigold flowers — welcoming the departed back, if only for one night, to enjoy the things they loved in life.

The Festival Ánimas Que Sí Amanezca was born from that tradition. Created by regional Mexican singer Alfredo Olivas, the festival carries special meaning for the artist: In 2015, he survived an onstage shooting that left him with multiple bullet wounds.

Life gave Olivas another chance — not only to live, but to become one of the genre’s biggest stars. This weekend, he honored the souls of the departed with a celebration at the Explanada del Estadio Akron in Guadalajara, Mexico. The grounds featured candlelit altars, giant Catrina figures and phone stations where festivalgoers could pretend to call loved ones who are no longer here.

The festivities began Sunday afternoon (Nov. 1) and carried on into the early hours of Monday (Nov. 2). Fans heard cumbia from Los Ángeles Azules , norteño from rising artist Moy Bobadilla, technobanda from Mi Banda El Mexicano and, of course, música de banda sinaloense and norteño banda from three of the genre’s biggest stars: Olivas, Edén Muñoz and Julión Álvarez .

Here are some of our favorite performances from the first edition of Ánimas Que Sí Amanezca.

With his face painted like a calavera, Moy Bobadilla took the stage to cheers and applause. The charismatic singer has seen his career take off this year with covers of songs from two decades ago. He even stepped into the crowd to sing, earning an enthusiastic response from fans.

Midway through his set, he shared a surprise announcement: “I want to let you know that very soon I’ll be releasing a collaboration with maestro Marco Antonio Solís, and I’m so happy.” The news comes after Bobadilla’s version of Solís’ “Cómo Me Haces Falta” went viral.

entertainment.title: NFL and TMRW Sports’ Set ‘Premier Flag’ League Launch for Summer 2027
entertainment.summary: The new league, with both mens and womens divisions, will launch ahead of the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, where flag football will be a sport.
entertainment.body:
The new flag football league from the NFL and TMRW Sports will officially launch next summer, and now it also has a name: Premier Flag.

The league and the sports media company (which is also behind the TGL golf league) announced the new branding Monday. Premier Flag will get underway well ahead of the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, where the sport will be prominently featured.

The NFL views flag football as a major growth engine, not only to get people interested in the full contact version of the game, but as a sport worth playing and watching in its own right. The inaugural season will be played in a purpose-built flag football stadium, the location of which is to be announced. Similarly, media rights for the first season are still being discussed, though the summer window gives it an opening, with only Major League Baseball as significant summertime competition (and a possible lockout may interrupt the next baseball season).

“Flag football is exploding in popularity, and Premier Flag is establishing itself as the destination for the world’s top women and men competing at the highest level of the sport. The Premier Flag brand represents where flag football is headed – elite, global and accessible – while setting a professional standard for the sport’s growing ecosystem,” said Brendan Donohue, president of flag football for TMRW Sports. “When we launch next summer, fans will have the opportunity to see these amazing athletes perform at their best, supported by Premier Flag’s world-class training, strength and conditioning, nutrition and coaching programs.”

“Premier Flag represents an exciting step forward in the continued evolution of flag football,” added Brian Flinn, NFL senior VP of global flag football. “Together with TMRW Sports, we’re building a global platform to showcase the world’s top flag football players and to engage fans in a premium experience, with the Premier Flag Showcase during Super Bowl LXI week providing an exciting first look at that vision. The launch of Premier Flag creates a new professional opportunity for the world’s best players and establishes the pinnacle of the sport’s growing global pathway.”

The NFL and TMRW Sports officially announced the league earlier this year, with all 32 team owners invested alongside institutional investors and celebrity investors like Silver Lake, Ariel Investments/Project Level, Bessemer Venture Partners, Blue Pool Capital, and Dynasty Equity, as well as Tom Brady, Peyton Manning, Serena Williams, Billie Jean King, Joe Montana and Alex Morgan.

entertainment.title: Mariah Carey Declares ‘It’s Time’ for Christmas 2026 With Holiday Campaign — and Another Grunge Album Tease
entertainment.summary: The Queen of Christmas has spoken!
entertainment.body:
It’s time! Mariah Carey has declared that the holiday season is upon us with her annual PSA, this year teaming up with a major fashion house for a festive campaign while also teasing the long-awaited release of her shelved grunge album (again).

For several years , the Queen of Christmas has heralded the beginning of the holidays with a video of herself singing in her signature whistle tones, “It’s time!” She kept with that tradition this year, sharing a cinematic sequence on Sunday (Nov. 1) of the calendar changing months. When it shifts to November, she appears in a bedazzled Santa-inspired jumpsuit and beams at the camera as the iconic opening bars of her evergreen smash “All I Want for Christmas Is You” twinkle in the background.

“IT’S TIME!!!!” she wrote in the caption, while her son, Moroccan, commented, “ITS FREAKING TIME YO.”

But fans shouldn’t let the Christmastime excitement distract them from the fact that in the first half of the PSA video — which shows what Carey supposedly got up to on Halloween this year — she appears in a colorful wig and punk makeup and fishnets while performing a thrashing number in a New York City dive bar. The song? “Hermit,” aka the centerpiece of Someone’s Ugly Daughter , Carey’s legendary grunge album that she recorded more than 30 years ago while working on 1995 album Daydream , but never properly released.

Fans have been begging Carey to free Someone’s Ugly Daughter from the archives for years, with the album currently existing only under the pseudonym Chick with Clarissa Dane on vocals instead of Mimi. In her Instagram video, Carey stage dives into the crowd just as the clock hits midnight, at which point the Christmas spirit takes her far away from the grunge scene — but could the nod to “Hermit” mean that Lambs may finally wake up on Christmas morning with Someone’s Ugly Daughter under the tree?

Possibly. Just a couple of days ago, Carey chatted with fans for a Reddit “Ask Me Anything” session, saying this to one person who inquired about the shelved LP: “I get asked this about once a week. my answer is…#notyet (this is a hint!)”

One day after the Christmas kickoff, the Songbird Supreme kept the holiday hype going by sharing her new partnership with Gucci. In the fashion house’s latest commercial, Carey makes a grand entrance at a snazzy hotel — the employees of which hastily decorate in the moments leading up to her arrival — and becomes the life of the party at a glamorous holiday party soundtracked by, yes, “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” The track has spent a collective 22 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 since its release in 1994, and with 2026 shifting into X-mas mode, it might just nab even more time at the top of the chart.

entertainment.title: Michael Jackson’s ‘Thriller’ Rides Halloween Boo-sts Back Onto Hot 100
entertainment.summary: It’s the Haunted 100, where “Thriller” is one of three returning occult classics.
entertainment.body:
Michael Jackson ’s “Thriller” lurches back onto the Billboard Hot 100 (dated Nov. 7) at No. 20.

Leading up to Halloween, the spooky anthem, and title track to Jackson’s landmark 1983 album, surged by 49% to 9.3 million chart-eligible streams in the United States Oct. 23-29, according to Luminate. It also doubled to 4.2 million in radio airplay audience and gained 61% to 3,000 sold.

“Thriller” originally hit No. 4 on the Hot 100 in March 1984, becoming the seventh and final top 10 from Jackson’s album that ruled the Billboard 200 for 37 weeks — the most for a set by a single artist. It also made the album the first with as many as seven top 10 songs.

The track by the King of Pop, who died in 2009, has returned to the Hot 100 each year this time since 2018. It first revisited the top 20 in 2021 and the top 10, hitting No. 10 , a year ago.

Two other Halloween-related hits creep back onto the Hot 100, led by Rockwell’s “Somebody’s Watching Me” at No. 39. It scared up 6.3 million streams (up 52%), 1.5 million in radio reach (up 49%) and 1,000 sold (up 58%) in the tracking week. The song — with backing vocals by Jackson — hit No. 2 in March 1984; it shared space in the top 10 with “Thriller” for three weeks that month.

Plus, Citizens of Halloween’s “This Is Halloween” reenters the Hot 100 at No. 41, led by 6.1 million streams (up 68%). The Danny Elfman-written song, which first made the chart in 2023 and rose to a No. 26 high last year, is from 1993’s beloved stop-motion animated film The Nightmare Before Christmas .

On the Streaming Songs chart, the titles with the six top percentage gains are all supernatural-themed, with “This Is Halloween” followed by Bobby “Boris” Pickett and the Crypt-Kickers’ “Monster Mash” from 1962 (up 63% to 5.8 million), Ray Parker Jr.’s “Ghostbusters” from 1984 (up 61% to 5.9 million), “Somebody’s Watching Me,” “Thriller” and Tame Impala and JENNIE’s “Dracula” — at its No. 5 high on the Hot 100 (up 11% to 7.2 million).

entertainment.title: The Longest-Leading Billboard Hot 100 No. 1s: ‘Choosin’ Texas’ & More
entertainment.summary: A select few hits have led the chart for at least 10 weeks — and 20-plus.
entertainment.body:
Beginning with Debby Boone’s “You Light Up My Life” in 1977, a relatively select few smashes have led the Billboard Hot 100 for at least 10 weeks. How few? Just a mere 4% of all Hot 100 No. 1s dating to the chart’s launch on Aug. 4, 1958, have earned the achievement.

Olivia Newton-John’s “Physical” flexed 10 weeks at No. 1 in 1981-82, and that smash and Boone’s shared the mark for the longest Hot 100 reign for more than a decade, until Boyz II Men’s “End of the Road” dominated for 13 weeks in 1992. That best lasted briefly, as Whitney Houston’s “I Will Always Love You” led for 14 weeks in late 1992/early 1993. In 1995-96, Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men’s “One Sweet Day” ran up 16 weeks at No. 1, a milestone that held for more than 23 years. (Songs began logging longer No. 1 stays after the Hot 100 adopted electronically tracked data, according to Luminate, in late 1991.)

In 2017, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s “Despacito,” featuring Justin Bieber, tied the No. 1 run of “One Sweet Day.” By 2019, Lil Nas X’s “Old Town Road,” featuring Billy Ray Cyrus, collected 19 weeks atop the Hot 100, a mark matched by Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” beginning in July 2024.

On the Sept. 5, 2026-dated Hot 100, Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” became the sole longest-leading non-holiday hit, with its 20th week at No. 1. As of the Nov. 7 survey, it’s the overall record holder with 26 weeks, having surpassed Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” which has jingled to No. 1 for 22 weeks over each holiday season since December 2019.

In honor of the singles that have claimed the Hot 100’s top spot the longest, here’s a look at the elite leaders to rule for double-digit weeks.

“It feels surreal,” Langley told Billboard News earlier in 2026 of the song’s impact. “I think this has been the biggest moment for me, where I’ve seen where fans can change your career. For so long, you’re like, ‘Alright, one song at a time, one record at a time.’ But with this one song — and they’ve done it continuously for me — but really with ‘Choosin’ Texas’ … man, have they taken ahold of it. It’s wild.”

entertainment.title: Marc Maron to Be Honored With Inaugural Richard Lewis Award at Comedy Gives Back Gala
entertainment.summary: The Richard Lewis Humor & Humanity Gala, dubbed "a night of comedy and neurosis," is set to take place at Hollywood Improv in Los Angeles on Nov. 15. Jeff Garlin will host and Nick Kroll will present.
entertainment.body:
Comedy Gives Back — a nonprofit founded by Jodi Lieberman, Amber J. Lawson and Zoe Friedman to provide a safety net for the comedy community — is finding another way to do so by launching its first ever gala in honor of the late Richard Lewis .

The Richard Lewis Humor & Humanity Gala, dubbed “a night of comedy and neurosis,” is set to take place at Hollywood Improv in Los Angeles on Nov. 15. The organization will present an inaugural trophy that night as well, also called the Richard Lewis Humor & Humanity Award, in honor of his legacy and his years-long commitment to uplifting his peers. They’ve settled on the first recipient, Marc Maron , who will be feted at the event, which will be hosted by Jeff Garlin and feature Nick Kroll as a presenter. Related Stories News Jeff Garlin Considered Suicide After Tumultuous 'Goldbergs' Exit General News Publicist Emily Vespa Joins Birch Public Relations

“Richard Lewis was one of a kind. He was fearless, painfully honest and could make you laugh about the things most people are afraid to talk about. To receive an award in his name is incredibly meaningful, especially knowing it supports comedians who need help,” said Maron in a statement.

Lewis, who passed away at age 76 in February 2024, was an early supporter of Comedy Gives Back and he served as a member of the org’s board. The fundraiser will host comedy and entertainment insiders while raising money for the mission of providing financial assistance, mental health resources and addiction recovery support for comedians in need.

“Richard wasn’t just a comedy legend. He was our friend and an early champion of Comedy Gives Back. We couldn’t imagine a more fitting first honoree than Marc Maron. This evening is about celebrating Richard’s incredible legacy while continuing his commitment to taking care of the comedy community,” said co-founders Lieberman, Lawson and Friedman in a joint statement.

Maron, a veteran stand-up and actor, launched his podcast WTF With Marc Maron in 2009. After 16 years, he stepped away to focus on other endeavors like his acting career. He stars in Stick and recently appeared in the Bruce Springsteen biopic, Deliver Me From Nowhere.
